text: I’ll model the fluid as the union of the 120 mm × 200 mm chamber and four horizontal rectangular duct volumes. Each duct centreline approaches the cylindrical wall at 15° from the local tangent and extends exactly 50 mm outward from its centreline’s wall-crossing point; I will extend it slightly into the chamber only to make a robust union. I interpret “40 mm above the floor” as the port centre height (an assumption to report). I’ll use a conformal unstructured mesh from the closed, patch-split fluid surface, starting with a coarse geometry preview.

The preview exposes one construction error: `Cylinder` defaulted to centred Z, giving −100 to +100 mm instead of floor 0 to top 200 mm. I will correct that before meshing. I also need the top face to be topologically split into a 40 mm outlet disk and the surrounding top annulus while keeping the boundary flush, so I’m checking the installed CAD API for a perimeter-based face split rather than inventing an outlet-pipe length.

The installed API supports splitting a face by a closed perimeter. I’ll rebuild at the correct elevation, split the top surface with the 20 mm-radius circle, and reconstruct the closed solid shell from the split faces. This keeps the outlet boundary flush at exactly 200 mm and avoids adding an unspecified neck.

The signature query confirmed that a `Shell` can be built directly from faces and a `Solid` from that shell; the failed lookup was only for a nonexistent convenience method. I’ll now perform the face split and verify closure, solidity, volume, and the two requested top areas numerically.

The reconstructed solid was created; the check failed only because this installed build123d exposes `is_valid` as a property rather than a method. I’ll repeat the self-contained reconstruction cell with the corrected validation call so the replayable build script contains the geometry definition.

The corrected fluid is one valid closed solid, and splitting preserved its volume exactly. Next I’ll inspect the final 28 boundary faces in design coordinates. This is to assign each duct’s terminal and four walls from its own axis and cross-section planes, while reserving cylindrical faces for the vessel wall—not by bounding-box position.

The face inspection revealed an important coarse-geometry issue: extending each near-tangential duct 35 mm inward carries its centreline back out through the curved wall, leaving an unintended second opening/cap. For a line 15° inward from tangent, maximum penetration occurs at \(R\sin15^\circ=15.529\) mm. I’ll terminate the construction blank there; its overlapping portion opens into the chamber, and any non-overlapping remainder is correctly part of that duct’s wall. Then I’ll classify the resulting faces in each duct’s local \((axis,width,height)\) coordinates and export all named patches together.

The union surface is closed and consistently wound, but the first classifier exposed a tagging defect: horizontal duct faces all share the same Z plane, so the “nearest boundary plane” tie incorrectly sent several to `duct1Walls`. The geometry itself is correct; I will fix ownership by requiring each face centre to lie within that duct blank’s local axis and width ranges, using normal alignment only to distinguish coincident candidates. Then I’ll re-export in one call.

The diagnostic confirms every duct-wall face has exactly one valid local-blank owner, so the corrected rule is unambiguous. I’ll apply it and overwrite the STL set; each of the four duct wall patches should then have the same four-face count and equal area by symmetry.

The corrected STL union has zero open, flipped, and non-manifold edges; all four duct-wall patches are now symmetric (five trimmed faces each). I’ll create a coarse 6 mm background mesh over the 165.2 × 165.2 × 200 mm envelope. SnappyHexMesh will retain the interior at `(0,0,0.1)`, snap to the named STL surfaces, and refine boundary cells once to about 3 mm.
The 31,500-cell background mesh is correct at 6 mm spacing. I’ll now run the coarse snap/refinement pass against the 12 exported patch surfaces, preserving every requested patch name.

Snappy stopped before altering the mesh because OpenFOAM 2512 requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for meshing. I’ll add those and repeat the self-contained snappy setup/run.

This version also parses standard scheme sections during mesh motion. I’ll provide the minimal complete finite-volume dictionaries and rerun; no solver fields or boundary conditions are being created.

The remaining failure is only an installation-path mismatch for the optional quality template. I’ll locate the OpenFOAM-supplied mesh-quality dictionary and then reference the installed path correctly (or inline it if needed).
The installed template is `caseDicts/mesh/generation/meshQualityDict.cfg` (with a `.cfg` suffix). I’ll switch the include to that exact name and rerun the coarse mesh.

The coarse snapped mesh completed with 33,108 cells and no final quality-control errors. I’ll run the binding `checkMesh` now and inspect patch face counts to ensure no named inlet, outlet, or wall disappeared during snapping.

`checkMesh` passes: one connected region, 12 boundary patches, max non-orthogonality 58.8°, max skewness 2.73, and positive cell volumes. All patches are nonempty and the four inlets/duct walls have symmetric face counts. I’ll now render the actual volume mesh with a clipped view so I can visually verify chamber connectivity and the four tangential ducts rather than relying only on statistics.

The clipped volume render shows the chamber interior and a connected tangential duct with refinement concentrated at the boundary; the symmetric patch counts establish the same connectivity for all four. Before completion, I’ll record direct CAD measurements for vessel diameter/height, each inlet rectangle and elevation, duct axis length/angle, and outlet diameter, alongside the meshed volume comparison.

All requested dimensions measure exactly, and the coarse mesh volume is within 0.095% of the CAD fluid volume. Since `export_patches` supports recording the interior point, I’ll refresh the identical STL/manifest set with `(0,0,0.1)` documented as the meshing point; this does not change the already checked mesh.

Completed the swirl-chamber gas geometry and mesh.

- CAD measurements: vessel ID **120.000 mm**, height **200.000 mm**, outlet diameter **40.000 mm**.
- Each inlet measures **20.000 × 30.000 mm**, has centre elevation **40.000 mm**, external axis length **50.000 mm**, and is **15.000°** off its local tangent.
- Assumption: “40 mm above the floor” means the **port centre height**.
- The outlet is a flush opening in the top; no unspecified outlet neck was added.
- Mesh: **33,108 cells**, one connected region, 12 nonempty named patches. Bare `checkMesh` reports **Mesh OK**, max non-orthogonality **58.76°**, max skewness **2.73**.
- CAD/mesh volume difference is **−0.095%**.
- The STL union has **0 open edges, 0 flipped edges, and 0 non-manifold edges**. All requested patch STLs are in `constant/triSurface`.
- I did not run a flow solver or create field boundary conditions.

The advisory coverage check confirms the desired result—every one of the 1,028 triangles belongs to exactly one of the 12 explicitly requested patches—but warns because the surface is highly partitioned. I am waiving that warning as correct for this patch-rich geometry; no geometry or mesh change is needed.
